h1: The 6 Best Transfer Boards for Car Use of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Transfer Boards for Car: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 transfer boards for car transfers scored on stated capacity, length, grip and turntable design, from wood to rotating discs.
summary: The DMI Wood Transfer Board is the best all-round board for most cars: 30 by 8 by 1 inches, a 440 lb stated capacity, sanded and sealed Scotch pine, two cutout handles and FSA eligibility. The Allvinda hardwood board gives the highest capacity at 500 lb in a shorter 24 inches. For users who benefit from a seated pivot, the LOSCHEN and Sienson turntable boards add a rotating disc.
intro: A car transfer is harder than a bed transfer because the geometry is against you. The seat is low or high, the door frame intrudes, the gap to the wheelchair is rarely level, and the board has to bridge it while taking weight at a slope. A board that is fine on a bedside can slip, tip or flex in a car, so the length, the surface and the way it grips both ends decide whether it is safe.

We ranked six transfer boards by their stated capacity, length, material, handles and grip features, and by whether a rotating disc or straps are included. These are mobility aids used with a caregiver or therapist in many cases, so ask an occupational therapist how to use a board with your car and your body before you rely on one.

products.name: DMI Wood Transfer Board 30 x 8 x 1 in
products.verdict: A sturdy Scotch pine board, 30 inches long, 440 lb stated capacity, with two cutout handles.
products.description:
The DMI board is sanded and sealed Scotch pine measuring 30 by 8 by 1 inches, with a 440 lb stated capacity, two cutout handles, and FSA eligibility.

It ranks first because it is the plainest, sturdiest design with a clear rating, and 30 inches spans most car-door gaps with a bit of margin at each end. The 1 inch thickness resists flexing under load better than the thinner 0.5 inch plastic boards. Cutout handles let a caregiver position it.

Buy it for standard car seats and drivers or passengers who want a simple wooden board. The caveat is that wood is heavier than plastic and slick surfaces can still be a problem with some clothing.
products.idealFor: Drivers and passengers who want a sturdy, simple wooden board.
products.skipIf: You need a rotating seat or a lighter board.

products.name: Allvinda Hardwood Transfer Board 24 in
products.verdict: A 500 lb hardwood board with a handle at each end, 24 inches long.
products.description:
Allvinda is a hardwood board measuring 24 by 8 by 0.75 inches with a 500 lb stated capacity, a handle at each end and a sealed, smooth surface.

It ranks second because the 500 lb rating is the highest here, but at 24 inches it is the shortest board, so it only works where the wheelchair can park close to the car seat. The DMI offers six more inches of span for less stated capacity. Hardwood and 0.75 inch thickness are a good strength-to-weight balance.

Buy it where the wheelchair can park close and capacity matters most. The caveat is the short length, which leaves little margin in a wide gap.
products.idealFor: Cars where the wheelchair parks close and capacity is the priority.
products.skipIf: You need to bridge a wide gap.

products.name: suboton ABS Transfer Board with Grip Pad 29.5 in
products.verdict: A thin 0.5 inch ABS board with three handles and a 10 inch non-slip pad.
products.description:
The suboton board is high-density ABS measuring 29.5 by 8 by 0.5 inches, with a 441 lb stated capacity, three handles and a 10 inch round non-slip pad.

It ranks third because the thin 0.5 inch profile slips under a narrow seat edge or onto leather more easily than a 1 inch wooden board, and the non-slip pad helps the user stay put. It costs more, at $50 to $100, and the plastic is lighter than the wood boards.

Buy it for cars with a narrow seat edge or leather seats. The caveat is that a thin plastic board flexes more than thick wood under load.
cons: Pad adds a part to clean
products.idealFor: Cars with a narrow seat edge or leather seats.
products.skipIf: You prefer a rigid wooden board.

products.name: LOSCHEN Slide Transfer Board with Turntable 29.5 in
products.verdict: A 29.5 inch ABS board with a 360 degree rotating disc, for assisted car transfers.
products.description:
LOSCHEN is a 29.5 by 8.9 by 0.9 inch ABS board with a 360 degree rotating disc with a textured surface and an anti-slip underside.

It ranks fourth because it lists no capacity, which is the first figure a transfer board should state. The rotating disc lets a seated user pivot toward the car seat without lifting their legs, which is the main advantage in a car. Its 29.5 inch length fits a trunk.

Buy it for assisted transfers where a rotating disc helps. The caveat is the missing capacity, so confirm the rating before use.
products.idealFor: Assisted car transfers where a rotating disc helps.
products.skipIf: You need a documented weight rating.

products.name: Sienson Rotating Turntable Transfer Board 35.4 in
products.verdict: A 35.4 inch turntable board for wide SUV and van gaps, rated 330 lb.
products.description:
Sienson is a 35.4 inch ABS board with a 330 lb stated capacity, a 360 degree turntable seat with an EVA pad and a grid anti-slip underside.

It ranks fifth because the 330 lb rating is lower than the DMI and Allvinda boards, and its length makes it awkward to stow. The length is its advantage: it spans the wider gaps at SUV and van seats, where a 30 inch board falls short.

Buy it for a taller vehicle and a user within the 330 lb limit. The caveat is the lower capacity and the long board.
products.idealFor: Wider gaps at SUV or van seats and users within the 330 lb limit.
products.skipIf: Your weight is near 330 lb or you have a small trunk.

products.name: YHK Plastic Transfer Board with Straps
products.verdict: A 308 lb ABS board with two adjustable buckle straps and an anti-slip back.
products.description:
YHK is an ABS board with a 308 lb stated capacity, two adjustable buckle straps, an anti-slip back and a blue finish.

It ranks last because 308 lb is the lowest stated capacity and the listing gives no length or thickness. The straps hold the board in place, which is useful, but they also add steps to a transfer and one more thing to check each time.

Buy it if you want the board strapped and you stay within the 308 lb limit. The caveat is that the dimensions are missing, so confirm the length for your car.
products.idealFor: Users who want the board strapped in place within the 308 lb limit.
products.skipIf: You need a higher rating or known dimensions.

methodology.title: Stated capacity
methodology.description: The weight rating the listing gives and how much margin it leaves.

methodology.title: Length and span
methodology.description: Board length against the gap between wheelchair and car seat.

methodology.title: Material and thickness
methodology.description: Wood or ABS and how well each resists flex.

methodology.description: Pads, anti-slip undersides, straps and handles.

methodology.title: Turntable design
methodology.description: Rotating discs that let a seated user pivot.

whatMatters.detail: The stated capacity is the load the maker rates the board for, and a board rated 308 lb offers far less margin than one rated 500 lb. Use the figure as a ceiling, not a target. Always check it on the listing, and choose a board whose capacity comfortably exceeds the user's weight.

A board must span the gap between the wheelchair and the car seat with overlap on both ends. A 24 inch board suits close parking, while a 35.4 inch board bridges SUV gaps. Measure the gap and add several inches at each end, and check that the board will fit in your trunk or back seat.

Wood boards of about 1 inch resist flexing, while thinner ABS boards slide under tight seat edges more easily. Thick wood is heavier, and plastic is lighter but flexes. Look for the material and thickness on the listing, and choose by whether your car has a narrow seat edge or a wide one.

A slick board can let clothing slide too far, while an anti-slip underside keeps the board from moving on the seat. Look for a named anti-slip back or pad on the listing, and check the board's ends for a firm hold on both the wheelchair and the car seat before any transfer.

A rotating disc lets a seated user pivot toward the car without lifting their legs over the door sill. It adds a moving part that needs checking, and it can make a user feel less stable. Ask a therapist whether a turntable suits you, and look for a stated rotation and a textured surface.

faq.q: Will a board fit my car?
faq.a: Measure the gap and add overlap. The Allvinda at 24 inches suits close parking, the DMI at 30 inches suits most cars, and the Sienson at 35.4 inches suits SUVs and vans. Check trunk space too.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake?
faq.a: Using a board without anchoring both ends. A board that slides is dangerous. The YHK has straps and the suboton a grip pad, but any board needs firm contact with the seat and the wheelchair.

faq.q: Is a turntable board worth it over a plain one?
faq.a: For some users, yes. The LOSCHEN or Sienson disc rotates 360 degrees, which helps a seated pivot. It adds a moving part, so ask a therapist before choosing it over the DMI.
Position the wheelchair close and lock the brakes, place the board under the thigh and onto the car seat, then slide across in small steps. A caregiver can steady it using the DMI's cutout handles.

faq.q: How do I look after it?
faq.a: Wipe with a mild cleaner and dry it. Check wooden boards like the DMI and Allvinda for cracks or splinters, and check ABS boards for stress marks. Replace any board that is damaged.

faq.q: Can I use the same board at home?
faq.a: Often, yes. A board for beds and chairs works similarly, and the DMI is FSA eligible. Car transfers add slope and door-frame limits, so test the board in your car with help first.

finalTake: Buy the DMI wood board for most cars: 30 inches, 440 lb stated and thick enough to stay rigid. The Allvinda is the high-capacity short board, the suboton suits narrow or leather seats, and the turntables suit people whose therapist recommends a pivot. Whatever you choose, practise the transfer with a caregiver before relying on it.
